abstract: Patescibacteria, also known as the Candidate Phyla Radiation (CPR), are among the most diverse yet functionally reduced bacterial lineages whose diversity in agricultural soils remains poorly characterized. We applied single-cell genomics to bulk soil from an unfertilized paddy field after rice harvest and drainage. From 384 randomly sorted single cells, 126 medium-to-high-quality SAGs (Single-Amplified Genomes) were recovered, spanning 24 bacterial and archaeal phyla. Unexpectedly, 108 of the 384 SAGs (28.1%) were assigned to Patescibacteria-the most frequently recovered phylum-including 42 of the 126 reliable SAGs. These genomes were notably small (mean 973 kb vs. 1.4-3.2 Mb for other phyla). Because CheckM underestimates completeness in reduced CPR genomes, CheckM2 was applied, raising mean completeness from 59.9% to 83.3% and reclassifying 15 genomes as near-complete (>90%). Phylogenomic analysis using 16 ribosomal protein markers revealed extensive diversity and low average amino acid identity to reference genomes (mean 44.6%), indicating substantial taxonomic novelty. Despite this diversity, functional annotation and OrthoFinder analysis showed a conserved, reduced gene repertoire dominated by translation and DNA repair genes and depleted in amino acid, cofactor, and nucleotide biosynthesis. These results show that modest soil sampling can recover outsized Patescibacteria diversity, underscoring the need for CPR-appropriate completeness assessment.
